candidates.attacker_control: HTTP request data: the hidden form field/parameter `t:formdata` (any POST to a page containing a Form) and the link/page parameter `t:state:client` (client-persistent fields), each consisting of an attacker-chosen HMAC prefix, a ':' separator, and an attacker-chosen gzip+base64 payload.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: The HMAC is computed over the entire base64-decoded payload (TapestryInternalUtils.copy reads to EOF, then Base64InputStream.reset() re-reads the same bytes), the check fails closed with IOException on mismatch (lines 119-133), and there is no unsigned/legacy fallback and only one ObjectInputStream construction site in the tree. GZIP decompression and object deserialization occur only after validation, so with a genuinely secret passphrase this path is not attacker-forgeable. The framework logs an error/warning when the symbol is unset, which mitigates only if operators configure it. Timing of the comparison (String.equals, line 129) is a separate, weaker concern.
candidates.impact: Forgery of server-authenticated client state and deserialization of attacker-controlled Java objects in the server JVM. With a suitable classpath gadget this is remote code execution; without one it still permits tampering with persisted field values/component actions and can trigger deserialization errors or resource exhaustion (the payload size is unbounded).
candidates.prerequisites: Application does not override tapestry.hmac-passphrase (the framework factory default is empty) or was generated from the quickstart archetype without changing the shipped literal; the attacker can guess/learn the application root package name (or knows the archetype literal). For code execution a serializable gadget chain (or abusable serializable Tapestry class) must be on the application classpath; otherwise the impact is state forgery/manipulation and deserialization-based denial of service.
candidates.root_cause: Tapestry authenticates serialized client-side state with HmacSHA1, but the key is derived from a non-secret value whenever the symbol is not configured: TapestryModule registers factory default tapestry.hmac-passphrase="", and ClientDataEncoderImpl falls back to the application package name (and logs only an error). The quickstart archetype AppModule instead hard-codes "change this immediately". Because the same code path then returns an ObjectInputStream over the (HMAC-tagged) payload, an attacker who can guess or knows this value can forge the tag and inject arbitrary serialized objects.
candidates.title: Guessable/default HMAC key protects signed client-side state, enabling forgery and unsafe Java deserialization
candidates.trace: Request parameter `t:formdata` -> Form.executeStoredActions (Form.java:696-741) -> ClientDataEncoderImpl.decodeClientData (line 82) -> Base64InputStream -> validateHMAC with hmacKey built at line 68 from the configured passphrase or the application package fallback (lines 50-65) -> reset + GZIPInputStream -> ObjectInputStream (line 112) -> ois.readObject()/action.execute(component) (Form.java:719-738). Same decode path from `t:state:client` -> ClientPersistentFieldStorageImpl.restoreMapFromClientData (lines 212-240) -> in.readObject() (lines 228-229).
candidates.unverified: No runtime testing, no generated HMAC payload, and no verification of actual deployment configurations. Not verified: how often real applications leave tapestry.hmac-passphrase unset or unchanged (the factory default is empty, so this is the shipped behavior until configured), whether the app root package name is externally discoverable for a given deployment, and whether a usable gadget chain is present for RCE. CVE/advisory mapping was not consulted (external lookups are out of scope).
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-1188/CWE-798 insecure default secret plus CWE-502 deserialization of untrusted data

coverage_summary: Read-only review of the assigned snapshot: 2070 files visible (source scope reports 0 excluded by binary/name/symlink filters, 0 over 5 MiB), of which the P1 index covers 2061 files (1821 Java parsed, 9 omitted/parse errors, 16190 unresolved calls, no control-flow or data-flow analysis, no semantic resolution; Spring annotation hints unverified). I examined in source the client-state subsystem (ClientDataEncoderImpl, ClientDataSinkImpl, Base64/Mac/Tee streams, Form, ClientPersistentFieldStorageImpl), the request/dispatch and link-encoding layers (ComponentEventLinkEncoderImpl, RequestSecurityManagerImpl, AssetDispatcher, ResourceStreamerImpl, ModuleDispatcher/ModuleManagerImpl), asset path screening (ContextAssetRequestHandler, ChecksumPath, ContextResource), whitelist/security helpers (ClientWhitelistImpl, LocalhostOnly), output escaping (AbstractMarkupModel, MarkupWriterImpl, MarkupUtils), upload/multipart, JSON, kaptcha, webresources, Hibernate/JPA grid data sources, and the build/archetype configuration. I did not exhaustively read all 1821 Java files; the bundled JavaScript assets and generated ANTLR parsers were not reviewed for vulnerabilities; no code was executed and no tests/scanners were run.
limitations: Static review only; no compilation, tests, or runtime confirmation was performed (per instructions).

The relation index provides syntax-level navigation only: no control-flow, data-flow, semantic resolution, reachability, or exploitability proof; 9 files are missing/parse errors and unresolved calls remain, so absence of a match in the index is not evidence of absence.

The candidate is configuration-dependent: its severity hinges on the application not setting tapestry.hmac-passphrase and on the attacker's ability to guess the application package name (or know the archetype literal), which I could not confirm for any concrete deployment.
RCE impact depends on a serializable gadget chain being present on the application classpath; this cannot be established from the snapshot.
No external advisory/CVE/ground-truth data was consulted, so the mapping of this finding to a specific disclosed vulnerability is unverified.

rejected_leads.lead: HMAC validation uses non-constant-time String.equals (ClientDataEncoderImpl.java:129), potentially allowing tag recovery by timing.
rejected_leads.reason: Byte-wise early-exit comparison of a 20-byte SHA-1 HMAC is theoretically weak, but recovery over HTTP requires per-byte timing resolution far below typical network jitter; no practical exploitation path is evidenced in source. Kept as a hardening note, not a separate candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: ContextAssetRequestHandler only screens WEB-INF/META-INF and *.tml by prefix (ContextAssetRequestHandler.java:38-55), so '..' segments are not explicitly rejected.
rejected_leads.reason: The resource path is passed to ServletContext.getRealPath/getResource, which mainstream containers normalize and reject when escaping the context root; no container-version evidence in the snapshot shows a bypass. Unconfirmed.

rejected_leads.lead: ModuleManagerImpl builds '/META-INF/modules/<moduleName>.EXT' from the URL path (ModuleManagerImpl.java:222-249), a potential classpath traversal.
rejected_leads.reason: The module name comes from the request path, but containers normalize/reject '..' path segments before dispatch, and only classpath resources are reachable. Unconfirmed.

rejected_leads.lead: Grid's client-persisted sort column id is used for model lookup without existence validation (Grid.java:373), and Form.isFormCancelled parses unvalidated JSON (Form.java:657-663).
rejected_leads.reason: Both can at most cause a runtime exception (500) for malformed input; no confidentiality/integrity/availability impact beyond noisy error handling.

rejected_leads.lead: Quickstart archetype ships a hard-coded passphrase ('change this immediately').
rejected_leads.reason: Same root cause as the submitted candidate (non-secret HMAC key for client state), so it is folded into that candidate rather than reported separately.

summary: Scope: Apache Tapestry 5.4.4-SNAPSHOT (2070 files; 1821 Java parsed; no binaries; per-file 5 MiB cap; 0 excluded by name/symlink filters). I surveyed request handling/dispatch, page-security and whitelist filters, asset/resource resolution, upload/multipart, JSON, kaptcha, webresources, and the client-state subsystem, then traced the strongest candidate end to end in source: Tapestry's client-side state (`t:formdata`, `t:state:client`) is authenticated with an HMAC whose key is not a secret by default, and the authenticated payload is then read with Java `ObjectInputStream.readObject()` and executed. The shipped factory default for `tapestry.hmac-passphrase` is the empty string; when it is empty, `ClientDataEncoderImpl` silently substitutes the application package name (a low-entropy, non-secret identifier) as the HMAC key, and the quickstart archetype ships the literal string "change this immediately" as the passphrase. Anyone who can guess/learn that value can mint valid client state and have the server deserialize attacker-chosen objects (sinks: Form component `t:formdata` -> readObject -> `action.execute(component)`; client persistent fields `t:state:client` -> readObject), i.e. unsafe deserialization with a forgery-enabled precondition. I found no unsigned/legacy fallback and no second `ObjectInputStream` site; the HMAC does cover the full payload and is checked before deserialization, so the weakness is the key material/configuration default plus the deserialization design, not the ordering of checks. Other leads (timing-unsafe HMAC `String.equals`, asset/module path handling, Grid sort DoS) were examined and rejected as weaker or unconfirmed. No runtime verification was performed.
